pl-l3d35c1-d1e115.summary: Turns to consider how wisdom differs from knowledge.

pl-l3d35c1-d1e118.summary: Quotes Augustine: the philosophers defined wisdom as knowledge of divine and human things, and both can be called wisdom or knowledge. But following Paul's 'to one the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge', knowledge of divine things is properly wisdom, of human things knowledge. Not everything humanly knowable, full of vanity and curiosity, belongs to this knowledge, only what generates, nourishes, defends, and strengthens saving faith. Many believers are strong in faith but lack this knowledge, for knowing what to believe differs from knowing how to help the pious and defend it against the impious.
claims: Wisdom properly concerns divine things, knowledge human things.
The knowledge that is a gift serves only to generate and defend saving faith.
Knowing what to believe differs from knowing how to defend it.

pl-l3d35c1-d1e133.summary: Adds Augustine on the Psalm, citing Job: wisdom is piety and knowledge is abstaining from evil. Piety here means the worship of God, theosebia, consisting in knowing and loving what always and unchangeably is, God; abstaining from evil means living prudently amid a wicked generation.
claims: Wisdom is piety, the knowledge and love of God.
Knowledge is abstaining from evil amid a wicked world.

pl-l3d35c1-d1e149.summary: Adds Augustine: contemplation of eternal things differs from the action by which we use temporal things well; the first is wisdom, the second knowledge, though wisdom can also be called knowledge, as in 'now I know in part'. So wisdom pertains to contemplation, knowledge to action.
claims: Wisdom pertains to contemplation, knowledge to action.

pl-l3d35c1-d1e161.summary: Concludes that the difference between the spirit of wisdom and of knowledge is shown: wisdom is attributed to divine things, knowledge to human.
claims: The spirit of wisdom concerns divine things; the spirit of knowledge, human things.

pl-l3d35c1-d1e164.summary: Adds, following Augustine, that we recognize both the divine and the human in Christ, and so have wisdom and knowledge from him: in 'the Word was made flesh', the Word is true Son of God and the flesh true son of man.
claims: Christ is the object of both wisdom and knowledge.

pl-l3d35c1-d1e176.summary: Adds: in 'we saw him full of grace and truth', grace refers to knowledge and truth to wisdom, since knowledge and wisdom were fully in Christ, and we have both from him who is God and man.
claims: Knowledge and wisdom were fully in Christ.
We receive wisdom and knowledge from Christ.

pl-l3d35c1.summary: Asks how wisdom differs from knowledge. Augustine: the philosophers defined wisdom as knowledge of divine and human things, but following Paul's distinction, wisdom is properly knowledge of divine things and knowledge (scientia) of human things, limited to what generates, nourishes, defends, and strengthens saving faith. Again, from Job, wisdom is piety, the worship of God, and knowledge is abstaining from evil; and wisdom belongs to contemplation of eternal things, knowledge to action in using temporal things well. Both are found in Christ, Word and flesh, from whom we have wisdom and knowledge, grace referring to knowledge and truth to wisdom.
claims: Wisdom is knowledge of divine things; knowledge (scientia) concerns human things.
Scientia includes only what serves saving faith.
Wisdom pertains to contemplation, knowledge to action.
Christ, God and man, is the object of both wisdom and knowledge.
